intro: Hatley is a pair of small villages, Hatley St George and East Hatley, in the clay farmland of South Cambridgeshire, about eighteen kilometres west of Cambridge. On Buff Lane, a farm track by a footpath sign, stands a big old tree a reader takes for an English elm, a rare survivor of Dutch elm disease, with a bone wedged in a crack of its trunk. They call it The Bone Tree.

question_answer: The Bone Tree of Hatley stands on Buff Lane near East Hatley in South Cambridgeshire, at a fork in the farm track beside a public footpath sign. It can be seen from the track at any time.
question_context: A reader walking near Hatley in South Cambridgeshire sent us this tree, on Buff Lane where a farm track forks beside a wooden footpath fingerpost. They take it for an English elm and call it a rare survivor of Dutch elm disease, which from the late 1960s killed most of the big hedgerow elms of lowland England. Their photograph shows a pale, deeply furrowed trunk that splits into two stems a few metres up and joins again before the limbs spread into a wide crown, with a second tall trunk beside it. In one of the cracks of the bark the reader found what they think is the leg bone of a fallow deer, and so they named it The Bone Tree; a second photograph shows the pale bone wedged upright in the fissure. We have no girth or age for it, and we would like someone who knows elms to confirm the species. The tree stands on the track itself, so it can be seen without going onto anyone's land. In winter the lane is deep mud, so wear boots.

faq.a: The reader who found it takes it for one. We have not confirmed the species; if you know elms, tell us what you see.

trees.story:
"A rare survivor or Dutch Elm disease resistant tree," wrote the reader who sent us this tree from Buff Lane near Hatley, in the clay country west of Cambridge. They take it for an English elm, and if they are right it is a rare thing: Dutch elm disease killed most of the big hedgerow elms of lowland England from the late 1960s on, and a tall elm with a trunk this thick is now hard to find.

The photograph shows it at a fork in a muddy farm track, a wooden footpath fingerpost leaning at its foot. A pale, deeply furrowed trunk climbs a few metres, splits in two, and, as the reader noticed, the two halves rejoin before the limbs spread out into a wide bare crown. A second tall trunk stands at its shoulder.

The reader also found something odd. "In one of the cracks is what I think is a fallow deer's leg bone," they write, "so I call it The Bone Tree." Their second picture shows it, a pale bone wedged upright in a fissure of the bark.

We have no girth or age for it yet, and we would like readers who know elms to confirm the species. If you pass, look for the bone in the crack, and leave it where it is.
